projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Florence Baudouine was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: We are recording today Florence Baudouine. This is January 16, 2004. The interviewer is Vicky Gadd. Okay, Florence.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, my contribution was strictly social. The USO opened the club in downtown Chicago and asked for volunteers to be hostesses and to prepare snacks and serve and play the piano. And since I had been playing the piano for what seemed like forever, I volunteered for that. And I did not play by ear, I brought big stacks of music and put them on the piano and people would pick out what they wanted to sing. And they had a concert grand piano, which would be surrounded by serviceman maybe three or four deep and singing up a storm. We had a wonderful time. And as I look back on it, I think I really was not impacted in a bad way by the war. For me it was a good time, and it was a time of development of personality and confidence. I was in my early 20s, and it just was a fun time. So I did that for I don't know how many years, but most of the time until the war ended and the ___ were down. But I also volunteered at a neighborhood serviceman center. We lived on the south side of the Chicago and there was a Naval base. There was a school for airmen or the engine workers and pilots, I assume, and they opened the neighborhood and I went there. When I wasn't downtown playing, I was over there. And, of course, when I was there, I lived within walking distance and I used to invite men home for dinner. My parents were very interested in having them and very hospitable. And my brother was in the service and was gone, and my mother used to say she hoped somebody else was feeding him and treating him like a son. I can't think any more.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Let me ask questions then. So then at the time of the war, were you in a relationship with anybody else that went to war? Were you married or single?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: No, I was single, and my husband and I belonged to a group out of our church, there were -- and all the boys went overseas, and so I wrote to all of them and sent care packages and developed a relationship with them and specifically with my husband. But he was gone two and a half years, and in those days they didn't get furloughs to come home or any relief from being over there, they just stayed. And so -- and we were very fortunate that the fellows in our group, we didn't lose any of them, and that was another reason why the war didn't impact me as much as it could have some people.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: So your brother must have come home.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: My brother came home; however, he didn't get home in time for our wedding. We were hoping that he would, but Chuck and my brother went through the Panama Canal about a week apart, and Chuck got to come back to New York City and be deployed and Keith went overseas in Okinawa, in that area?

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: I do recall discussing that in Chuck's interview, too.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: So then you -- how old were you at the time?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I was probably 21, 22. I was in college, going to a teacher's college when Pearl Harbor happened, and I was supposed to graduate in January of '42, and because so many of the Chicago teachers joined up and left, they accelerated our courses and we were graduated around the 18th of December, and right after Christmas we started substitute teaching in Chicago. And at that time in Chicago you did not get assigned to any specific school for about two years, so we substituted all that time. So substituting was not my favorite thing. It's not an easy job, especially in a big-city school. And so many of the schools were in the poorer districts, and it was not something I was used to, and I ended up going and working in an office instead, and I was -- I think I started in the USO in 1942, but I'm not sure, so that was what carried me through all those difficult times.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: So why did you choose that activity in the USO?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, I had already played the piano for practically everything I could think of. I played in a dancing school for quite a while, and I just liked to do it and was proficient at it, so I thought I would be able to do it. And I think when I look back, it was kind of a crutch for me, a social crutch because I was not very sophisticated, and I wasn't a beauty or anything, so I leaned on the piano for my social activities and I enjoyed it. I really did. I liked to sing and play.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: What did you like about it the most do you think?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I think it was a congeniality, and some of the fellows would come back time after time because they liked to sing, you know, and they would get a group harmonizing, and so it was something that they could do when they had free time, something they liked to do, and I did, too. I bought a lot of music for choirs because it was cheaper, for one thing. I remember sheet music was about three or four copies for a dollar at that time, and I think it's $2.50 or $3.75 now. So I would buy the handbook for choir and it would have the parts written out, and so we did a lot of singing and harmonizing, and that was fun.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: That does sound like fun. And then when you were -- so that was downtown Chicago. And then when you were at the --

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: The local one?

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: -- yeah, the local one, did you -- you played the piano there also?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, I did some, but there was another boy in the neighborhood that was blind and he played by ear, and he did most of the playing so I probably did more socializing and dancing at that one.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: And you said your brother was in the war. How did your family react to that?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, I only remember my mother being so worried about him and concerned. And here I was seeing the good side of things, the social side and I wasn't even -- I don't think I was even imagining what he might be going through, but my mother certainly was. We did a lot of entertaining at that time. And even downtown I would put out the word that I could invite four servicemen to come home with me for dinner or to come by themselves on a holiday or something like that, so we did a lot of entertaining, and we heard a lot of interesting stories by those fellows.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: I bet. Do you remember any, like, that stand out?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I was thinking about one. At that time women -- you know, there was the women's auxiliary, Army Auxiliary Corps, WAAC, and they were called WAACs and there was auxiliary to the Coast Guard, and one of them the fellows was telling us about the Russian women who were pilots, and they were flying (chips) over the North Pole I would say, in that area, and getting them from Canada or the U.S. and bringing them back to Russia, and that seemed really advanced to us to think of a woman pilot because -- well, I thought of joining one of the auxiliaries and wrote to my brother about it, and he said, "No, don't do that," and I really don't know his reasoning, but I took his word for it and didn't consider it anymore. I don't think I was too anxious anyway. I thought it might be the right thing to do, but...

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: The right thing to do like in order to be one to help, you wanted to help?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Right. Like the boys were enlisting instead of waiting to be drafted, and it was our age group that was going, so I guess I thought I might want to get on the band wagon and do it, too. And I do have a good friend who was in the WAACs, and she said all that was different was that she lived in kind of a dormitory setting and worked in an office, so there it was nothing that unusual, but you really didn't know what you were going to get into.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: And then how else did your life change because of the war, like, as far as activities, habits, you know, like rationing, things like that?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, we did a lot of that. As a teacher, I was in the group that signed up people to get their ration books, and I remember in particular one lady who came and she had small children with her and she was very pregnant, but I don't think I was terribly aware of that until she told me that she was going to deliver any time, and I just wanted to get her out of there and not have it right there. But it was hard sometimes making ends meet, and I wonder sometimes how my mother did it when she invited all these extra people to come for meals. But she was quiet and just did what she needed to do and didn't make a big fuss about it. And I remember particularly substituting margarine for butter, and we didn't -- they didn't have the colored margarine like they do now. You would buy it in a bag and break a little capsule of color and knead it in and it was pretty spotty, but we did that for a while afterwards, too, and margarine wasn't as good then as it is now either. But I remember flattening cans and taking the labels off and recycling them and just doing a lot of collecting, and it was good for the environment as well for the cause. But I think that they make cans out of different materials these days and they're not recyclable.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Did you ever have to do any, like, type of tests or drills or turn off your lights at night or things like that?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: We did a little of that. We had neighborhood wardens, and they checked -- if we were to go dark, they would come around and check, but we weren't involved in that, my father wasn't.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: What part of Chicago did you live in?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: We were on the southeast side of Chicago.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: What was the name of the area?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: South Shore. We could walk to the lake, and it really was a nice area to be in. That's where I grew up. I lived there from the time I was three years old until my daughter was three years old. We had built an apartment in the house -- housing was very tight at the end of the war when the fellows started coming and starting families. I remember Dad built this apartment for me in what had been my bedroom before, and it was a nice little apartment. There was a lot of that type of building going on. But my brother and his wife had a terrible apartment we thought. It was in a real old building upstairs over a store and it was real grungy and dark, and he wasn't there terribly long. Then my folks moved out to Portage and my brother moved into the downstairs of our house and we had the upstairs and we made do with what we had.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Could you tell me about corresponding with friends via letters or packages? How did you do that?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, I kept up the correspondence with a lot of the servicemen that I knew, and my mother and I baked and then we would make packages and pack things up and send them. And we found out that cookies didn't travel too well. It was better to put -- I think we put fudge in cans, used cans and we would pack them with fudge. That seemed to go over well because of the traveling.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Did you send them to friends of yours from your neighborhood?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: No, these were mainly from that group that I belonged to that I mentioned before and they were our closest friends, mine anyway, and, of course, I sent them to my brother, and he had friends that we had known for quite a while. My parents were very generous people. They didn't have much, but they shared it with others.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Do you think medical care changed because of the war?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Yes, I do. I remember hearing that a lot of innovations were used in -- they may have been the same since they had to do because they couldn't do what they were used to doing and they turned out to be better. I'm thinking of saving limbs and so forth. A lot of innovations. If there was anything good that came out of it, I guess that would be the top?

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: And what do you think your most memorable experience was?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, I remember playing the piano with the USO at Christmastime and everybody was homesick and still they wanted to sing all the Christmas carols that they were used to singing, and it was so hard because I looked up and could see all these fellows standing around crying and singing and it made a big impact?

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Were there any of them that kind of stood out more than others, any people that you met there?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, they came and went so fast that you really didn't get to be real well acquainted with anybody. But I remember one funny thing that happened. My brother had told me one time when I -- oh, a fellow got too friendly on the street car, and he said, "Well, if that happens again, you put your elbow in their side and make a fist and then hit it with your other hand," and he said, "He'll feel it?" Well, I was playing the piano and sitting on the piano bench and a sailor came and sat beside and he started to pound on the keys, and everybody was getting very annoyed, and I guess he thought it was real funny, so I put my elbow in his rib and hit my hand, and he flew off the bench. It surprised all of us.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Yeah. Him especially.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: But he had rolls on and on the polished bench, he just went right off.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Funny.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I didn't have any idea that was going to happen so it was funny.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: He got what he deserved.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Yeah. He behaved after that.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Let's see. Did you have a victory garden at your house?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Oh, yes, we had a victory garden. We had a plot in the backyard about -- the backyards were small in our neighborhood and we only had about, oh, I'd say maybe 10-foot by 12-foot square so you couldn't grow a whole lot, but we did what we could. And if we could get enough gas we would go up to Michigan and buy fruits and vegetables by the bushel and then come home and can them. We did a lot of canning, mother and dad and I, and that was kind of a fun thing to do. And we sang while we did it. My mother and dad and I sang together a lot for the fun of it, and I found out later when I got ahold of piece of music that dad was making up the words. He was very inventive about it, but it was a fun time. But as I look back now, it's just amazing to me that it wasn't more traumatic for me. You know, I wasn't aware of what was going on.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: When we're young, we don't understand.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: When you're so removed from it.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: And we didn't have it in the papers like they do now either.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: How did you feel about it if you heard it from news reels or radio? Did you pay a lot of attention to that?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Did you, like, your parents and everybody listen to --

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Yeah, we listened to the radio.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Was that scary at all?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I don't think I was around a lot while they listened. I was gone. As I said, it didn't impact me as much and now -- well, in the years of Korean and Vietnam I realized more what was going on, even though I didn't have anybody directly involved. I know I was just glad that my boys were too young to go. It's amazing to me that I escaped most of that trauma.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Tell me about corresponding with Chuck while he was over there and all that, how you kept that relationship going.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, he was just one of the half dozen that I was writing to, and as he told you, you know, I probably signed a letter "love" instead of "always" or something like that that I might have used, you know, and that meant something to him. But I wrote to other boys, too, and they couldn't tell you much about what they were doing at all. And I remember getting letters that were sent to me cut right out of the page. You couldn't tell what it was. Chuck picked up a picture of me that I sent him and mistakenly put it in a letter to his parents, and it didn't have my name on it, but his father figured that he had done that intentionally because my name is Florence to indicate that he was in Italy, which he was, so he kind of figured that out. Of course, our letters were not sensored so he could write and ask him a question and get a yes or no answer, so that was basically how they found out where he was. I remember him writing and telling about living with a family there and how difficult it was to get along because of the language barrier. And my brother was in Germany a lot and he had the same problem. And there was another friend that I wrote to in India, and he mentioned that they called all the men "sahi" -- I think that's what it is, and it was like mister, I suppose, or sir, a sign of respect. And then we found out later that all of this was kind of connected, that the materials that Chuck was sending out was used by another...____+

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Do you remember where you were when you heard the news that the war ended?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: No. I knew -- I had a lot on my plate. Pearl Harbor was so -- such a strong --

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: I bet that was comparable to 911.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Yes, it was in our minds. And we didn't realize until quite a while afterwards.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Nowadays we know that stuff instantly.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I don't know if that's good or not. It's so traumatic to get that kind of news. I remember 911 I just was wanted to know what was going on because it was available, but not wanting to know because it hurt so bad.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: So I think we had a little of that in Pearl Harbor. It surely changed our lives because of our age.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: So after the war, what did you do? You just got back to your regular activities or how did that go?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, we were engaged as soon as he came home and married three months, so life changed drastically, and I think I got pregnant on my wedding night and I was sick as a dog, so talk about change, yes, and we moved away, too. And I had never been away from home. I was really a home body, and I didn't go away to school, I went to a city college, so that was a rough time. And housing was not really available in a college town, and we had three rooms in the upstairs of an old house, a family lived downstairs and we shared the bathroom and I remember how sick I was. I was surprised when I went to the doctor and he announced I was pregnant. I didn't even think of that. That was far from my mind.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Now, how did -- tell me about Chuck coming home and where you -- you know, how was that arranged. He was from your neighborhood anyway.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Yes. We were from the same neighborhood.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: So did you meet him when he got off the train or whatever?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: No, I stayed out of it because he had sent me a telegram from down in Panama to tell me he was coming back, and I got mine before his folks got theirs, and I called them right away, because I was friendly with the family, and I called his mother, and she was a little disappointed to think that I got the word first, you know, and so I kind of backed off and I didn't press it at all because we weren't engaged then and I don't think we were even thinking about being engaged.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Oh, okay. So you didn't start talking about marriage until after he got back, and then you got married within three months.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: He came home in August and we were engaged in September, and we were engaged on the day that our son-in-law was born. I said that was kind of prophetic when I found out it was that very day. We didn't waste any time after that, and all our friends were getting married. This group that we belonged to, there were several couples out of that group that married and we're still in touch with them.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: They're all over the country. They're in San Diego and Phoenix and Illinois, Louisville, Kentucky, and one stayed in the Chicago area.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Do you -- is there one thought about the war time experience that you want to share with future generations?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I don't know. I think just to keep informed and to keep in touch with people who are gone because I think that's really important. Our church has a ministry going on right now where we have a little notebook for each service person whose name is put in and we share these, pass them around and just write our thoughts about what they're doing and how much we appreciate it and then they will get those books when they get back.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Fantastic. Oh, that's great.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: And it kind of shows that life goes on no matter what's happening overseas. We're still celebrating birthdays and Christmas and anniversaries, and people are dying, and, you know, we're mourning -- everything is normal here compared to what they're going through. I don't have the faintest idea what they're going through.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Yeah. Why does that upset you? Just a tender-hearted person?

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I know of twin sisters who are both married and one has a baby, I guess, a little girl about three years old, and both of these girls are in the service and both of them are overseas and their parents are trying to cope with everything here.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Wow. Oh, that would be so difficult.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I don't like to see the women go in the service, not that I think they can't handle it or -- there's a lot of women who would do just as well as the men, but if they're mothers, I don't think they should be there.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: I agree. If they're mothers --

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I just don't think they should be.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: No, I don't either. And I know they sometimes don't have that choice because they become mothers after they've already joined, and unexpectedly.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Well, our granddaughter is 19, I think, and she is in the Army because she went into the ROTC in high school and did it because she wanted to get a college education, and she knew her family couldn't afford it, her parents are divorced, and so she went in the Army. Of course, I think the ROTC is a recruitment anyway. So she's over in Hawaii, which isn't a bad place to be, but for a long time when she first went over there they were saying that they were going to ship those people to Korea, so that's what we were thinking all the time, but that doesn't seem to be the case.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Well, that's good.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: She's going to college now. I got to talk to her. She was home for the holidays and she called and she said she does her regular Army routine during the day and goes to night school. And I think that's good because it keeps them occupied at night and that's probably the time they're apt to get into trouble, you know, when they're free from their duties, so I'm glad to hear that she's going to school.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: But now her younger sister has joined the ROTC, and I just can't imagine both of these girls, they probably each weigh about 90 or 100 pounds, just little girls.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I can't imagine having somebody right in the thick of it.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: I know. That would be difficult.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: And I was alarmed to read about the suicide rate, how high it is in the Army.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: And I don't think that's something they talked about, you know.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: And other wars there probably was the same thing, but we never heard about it.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: I haven't heard much about that myself.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: I know the people that went to Korea and Vietnam were traumatized but --

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: I know. Definitely.

sp.speaker: Florence Baudouine
sp.p: Now your generation was probably affected by that.

sp.speaker: Vicky Gadd
sp.p: Vietnam, yeah. By Vietnam, to a certain degree. I graduated from high school in '74 and... (End of audio)
